content.text:
You are a Capcom NES animator (Mega Man 2-3). The image shows the 2 frames available for an enemy,
left to right (enlarged; the grey-blue background is not part of the sprite). Frame 1 is the still.

The enemy: A small floating robot squid, Blooper-like, that swims along at and after Mega Man in pulses (tentacles gather, then thrust). It is a swimming mine: when it gets close its eyes flash red, then it explodes.
Its behaviour in the game: moves toward Mega Man in pulses about every 40 game frames: a short gather (tentacles flare, a brief tell), then a quick stroke that shoots it forward and a long glide that slows down with the tentacles together

Its states: "float" shows the still (frame 1) with no animation; how long it floats is decided by the behaviour,
not by you. You are timing the "swim" state, a oneshot action: one pulse: the tentacles flare out wide (the gather), then snap back together as it shoots forward, returning to the still

Design the action as a sequence of frames to show, each with how long it is held in game frames at 60 fps (whole
numbers). The action plays once; afterwards the enemy is back on the still (frame 1), so do not include the float
hold. Capcom NES enemies hold action frames for roughly 4-16 game frames; tells (a pose that warns the player) are
held long enough to read.

Return ONLY a JSON object: {"sequence": [{"frame": n, "duration": n}, ...], "rationale": "one or two sentences"}

message.content: {"sequence":[{"frame":2,"duration":16},{"frame":1,"duration":8}],"rationale":"Frame 2 (tentacles flared) is the gather, held 16 game frames so the player can read the tell. It then snaps to frame 1 (tentacles together) for the 8-frame thrust, and the behaviour's glide continues on that same still pose."}
message.reasoning: I see two frames for the swim cycle: frame 1 has tentacles trailing together, frame 2 has them flared wide as a gathering tell before snapping back to frame 1 for the forward stroke. The pulse cycle repeats roughly every 40 frames, combining the gather and stroke phases.
